The museum licenses her to paint in the gallery on Tuesdays.
She has completed forty-three copies of the same portrait.
She can identify precisely what is wrong with her most recent copy.

why.A: Correct — this is the one detail showing her observations changing a decision made by someone else.
why.B: The license grants her access; it says nothing about whether her findings are used.
why.C: The count establishes her persistence, not the usefulness of what she learned.
why.D: Her self-criticism demonstrates her precision but stays inside her own practice.

context: Which detail best supports the passage's claim that copying was once central to how paintings were encountered?

choices.text: A painting's reputation in Antwerp depended on the quality of the copies that reached Madrid.
Painters we now call original were often the best copyists of their generation.
The Romantics elevated originality into the central virtue of art.
The background of the portrait is three colours rather than one.

why.A: Correct — it shows copies carrying a work's reputation between cities, which is precisely the claim that copies were how paintings were seen.
why.B: This supports copying's role in training and skill, not in how audiences encountered work.
why.C: This describes the attitude the passage is arguing against, not evidence for copying's former centrality.
why.D: This is a finding from Obregón's own practice and has no bearing on historical reception.

context: The third paragraph, which describes "a chain" of estimated numbers, primarily serves to:

choices.text: explain why the uncertainty in the population figure accumulates rather than arising at one step.
argue that the researchers have chosen an unnecessarily complicated method over a simpler one.
establish that the tagging studies are the weakest of the several links in the procedure.
introduce acoustic monitoring as the answer to the problems the paragraph has just described.

why.A: Correct — the paragraph walks through three separate assumptions, each carrying its own estimate, to show that the final figure inherits uncertainty from all of them.
why.B: The previous paragraph argues the method is forced by arithmetic, not chosen carelessly.
why.C: Tagging is one link among several, and the paragraph singles none of them out as the weakest.
why.D: Acoustics does not appear until two paragraphs later, and the passage says it cannot count.

context: Which choice best describes the function of the second paragraph in relation to the first?

choices.text: It answers an objection the first paragraph invites by showing the constraint is physical rather than human.
It provides the statistical detail that supports the most cited figure of about thirty animals.
It introduces a disagreement among researchers about how the surveys ought to be designed.
It narrows the passage's subject from right whales generally to the eastern population.

why.A: Correct — the first paragraph says the survey effort "would embarrass a pollster," and the second replies "This is not carelessness. It is arithmetic," then shows why exhaustive coverage is impossible.
why.B: The second paragraph explains why counting fails; it offers no support for that particular figure.
why.C: No disagreement between researchers is described anywhere in the passage.
why.D: The first paragraph has already named the eastern population, so there is nothing left to narrow.

context: The passage is organized primarily as:

choices.text: a problem, the reasons it resists a direct solution, a partial advance, and what remains unresolved.
a chronological history of right whale surveys from the nineteenth century to the present day.
a comparison of two competing survey methods, ending in an endorsement of the newer one.
a case study of a single survey voyage, generalised into a broader principle about counting.

why.A: Correct — the passage opens on the unknown number, explains why direct counting is impossible, presents acoustics as a real but partial gain, and closes on what is still unknown.
why.B: No history of past surveys is given; the time references illustrate the arithmetic rather than a sequence.
why.C: Acoustics is presented as complementary and explicitly unable to count, so it is not endorsed over ship surveys.
why.D: No individual voyage is described; the forty-year figure is a calculation, not a trip.

context: The author's attitude toward the researchers' population estimate is best described as:

choices.text: accepting of its usefulness while insisting on the limits of what it can claim.
dismissive of a figure produced by fieldwork the author considers inadequate.
confident that acoustic monitoring has now made the population figure reliable.
indifferent to a technical dispute the author regards as having no practical stakes.

why.A: Correct — the author writes that "None of this means the number is worthless" and then insists it is "a conclusion, not an observation."
why.B: The author explicitly rejects that reading: "This is not carelessness. It is arithmetic."
why.C: Acoustics is said to establish where whales are, while counting "remains unsolved for this species."
why.D: The final sentence stresses that the stakes are enormous if the number turns out to be wrong.

context: The phrase "somewhere uncomfortable and honest" conveys the author's view that the field has:

choices.text: gained real knowledge while becoming more candid about what it still cannot measure.
reached an impasse that makes further work on the population figure hard to justify.
allowed pressure from managers to distort the figures it reports publicly.
abandoned ship surveys in favour of a newer method it does not fully trust.

why.A: Correct — the sentence that follows says the field knows more about where the whales are and not much more about how many, which is exactly a gain paired with an admitted limit.
why.B: The passage describes acoustics as a real advance rather than a dead end.
why.C: No distortion is suggested. Managers use the best available number, and the passage says so plainly.
why.D: Nothing indicates ship surveys have been abandoned; acoustics is added to them, not substituted.

context: The comparison of the survey effort to something that "would embarrass a pollster" is used to:

choices.text: convey how small the sample is relative to the area it is meant to represent.
suggest that whale researchers lack training in statistical sampling.
imply that public opinion polling is a more rigorous discipline.
criticize the funding agencies that limit time at sea.

why.A: Correct — the clause is immediately followed by the scale of the mismatch: a handful of ships and a few weeks against an ocean the size of a continent.
why.B: The next paragraph attributes the limitation to arithmetic rather than to the researchers' skill.
why.C: Polling is invoked as a familiar yardstick for sample size, not held up as superior.
why.D: Funding is never mentioned in the passage.

context: Which detail most directly supports the claim that exhaustive ship-based counting is impractical?

choices.text: Covering the eastern North Pacific with one vessel would take roughly forty years.
The most cited figure for the eastern population is around thirty animals.
Right whales gather where their prey gathers, and prey is not evenly spread.
A moored recorder can listen for a year rather than for a few weeks each summer.

why.A: Correct — a survey that outlasts the population it measures is the passage's direct demonstration that the approach cannot work.
why.B: The figure is the disputed output of the method, not evidence about whether the method is feasible.
why.C: Uneven distribution undermines an assumption inside the reasoning, but says nothing about how long a survey would take.
why.D: This describes the advantage of the alternative method rather than the limits of the ship-based one.

context: Which detail best supports the claim that acoustic monitoring has genuinely added to what researchers know?

choices.text: Recorders have shown right whales present in parts of the Bering Sea in months no survey has covered.
Right whales call, and recorders keep working in darkness, fog and heavy weather.
A hundred recorded calls may come from one talkative animal or from twenty quiet ones.
A responsible population estimate is published as a range spanning roughly a factor of three.

why.A: Correct — this is a specific fact established by recorders that no previous method had produced.
why.B: This explains why recorders are capable, which is a precondition for the finding rather than the finding itself.
why.C: This states the limitation of acoustics, which is the reason it cannot yet count rather than a contribution.
why.D: The published range describes the uncertainty of the ship-based estimate and predates the acoustic work.

context: Which detail most directly supports the idea that the assumption about how whales distribute themselves is imperfect?

choices.text: Whales gather where their prey gathers, and prey is not evenly distributed either.
A whale must be at the surface in order to be seen.
Detection rates are measured in conditions unlike those of an actual survey.
Distinguishing individual whales by voice remains unsolved.

why.A: Correct — the passage names this as the reason the even-distribution assumption is "false in detail."
why.B: Surfacing time affects whether an animal is visible, a separate link in the chain.
why.C: Detection rates concern the observer's reliability, not how whales are spread across the ocean.
why.D: This is a limitation of acoustics and unrelated to the distribution assumption.

context: In describing the cabinets as "a museum with no curator," the narrator most nearly means that the contents were:

choices.text: carefully preserved by someone who was no longer there to explain them
valuable enough that a museum would have wanted to acquire them
neglected for years and left in disorder
arranged deliberately for visitors to walk through and admire

why.A: Correct — the museum half of the comparison captures the deliberate order the narrator finds, while the missing curator captures the absence of the one person who could say what any of it meant.
why.B: The comparison is about how the objects were kept, not what they were worth; nothing suggests the flour tins and buttons had market value.
why.C: This ignores the museum half entirely. The narrator finds flour in labeled tins and buttons sorted by color, which is the opposite of disorder.
why.D: Perpetua lived alone and kept the cabinets for herself. The comparison points to preservation, not display.

context: The narrator's comparison of the house to a shell, "the way a shell is a container for whatever lives inside it," functions in the passage to:

choices.text: state a belief the narrator goes on to reverse
explain why the house was built the way it was
emphasize how fragile the old house had become
suggest that Perpetua felt trapped in the house

why.A: Correct — the narrator introduces the shell comparison as what she "had believed" and immediately says she had it backward: Perpetua was keeping the house, not being kept by it.
why.B: The comparison describes a relationship between person and house, not architecture or construction.
why.C: Shells can suggest fragility, but the narrator uses this one for the idea of containing, and the house in this passage is anything but delicate.
why.D: The passage reverses the containment idea rather than developing it into confinement; Perpetua is shown as the active keeper.

context: The phrase "that thin, upright script that leaned into the wind of the page" characterizes Perpetua's handwriting as:

choices.text: narrow and slanted, as though pressing forward against resistance
faded by age to the point of near illegibility
hurried and careless, made without attention
unusually large and looping across the paper

why.A: Correct — thin and upright describe the letters themselves, and leaning into a wind supplies the slant along with a sense of effort directed against something.
why.B: Nothing in the description concerns fading or legibility; the narrator reads the labels without difficulty.
why.C: Labeled tins and sorted buttons establish care, and an upright script leaning deliberately is not a careless one.
why.D: Thin and upright are the opposite of large and looping.

context: The narrator compares the six wooden spoons to "a set of parentheses waiting for something to enclose" primarily to convey that the spoons:

choices.text: share a matching curve that now surrounds nothing
were kept as a complete set and never separated
had been damaged in a way that made them unusable
were arranged in pairs rather than as a group of six

why.A: Correct — the spoons are all worn on one side and curved the same direction, and parentheses that enclose nothing carry the sense of something absent, which the closing paragraph confirms when they sit in a drawer "still waiting."
why.B: That the set is complete is stated plainly elsewhere; the comparison is doing the work of shape and absence, not of completeness.
why.C: The wear is evidence of long use, and the narrator keeps and stores them, so usability is not the point.
why.D: Parentheses come in pairs, but the narrator describes all six laid side by side, not sorted into pairs.

context: By describing her mother's reaction as "a small exhale that in our family does the work of an entire paragraph," the narrator suggests that:

choices.text: a wordless sound communicates a great deal among people who know each other well
her mother had been rehearsing a long speech about the house
her mother was too out of breath from other work to say much
the family prefers writing to speaking when a subject is difficult

why.A: Correct — the sound is small, the narrator recognizes it immediately, and its stated effect is that of a paragraph, so brevity is carrying a large amount of shared meaning.
why.B: Her mother's actual words are two short remarks; nothing suggests a prepared speech.
why.C: An exhale here is an expressive sound, not a sign of physical exertion, and the phone call gives no hint of either.
why.D: The comparison to a paragraph is a measure of how much is conveyed, not a claim about a preference for writing.

context: The statement that "Perpetua's English arrived late and never fully unpacked" treats her language as though it were:

choices.text: a traveler who came to stay but never quite settled in
a skill she abandoned before completing it
a possession she deliberately kept hidden from her family
a burden she was forced to carry against her will

why.A: Correct — arriving and unpacking belong to someone who travels to a new place, and the sentence goes on to describe sentences that "took the long way around," extending the same idea.
why.B: She used English daily in speech and writing, so the comparison is about how it settled rather than whether she stopped learning.
why.C: Nothing suggests concealment; the narrator reads her labels and recipe cards freely.
why.D: Unpacking implies arrival and settling, not compulsion, and the passage treats her English with affection rather than resentment.

context: The narrator describes the evening light as moving "the way water finds the low places" in order to emphasize the light's:

choices.text: slow, unhurried spread across the room
unusual coldness at the end of the day
tendency to damage the old floorboards
sudden appearance after a long absence

why.A: Correct — the sentence already says the light came across the floorboards slowly, and water settling into low ground is a gradual, inevitable motion that reinforces it.
why.B: The comparison is to how water moves, not to how water feels; temperature is not at issue.
why.C: Water can damage floors, but the point of comparison here is the manner of the movement, and nothing in the passage reports damage.
why.D: Finding the low places is a gradual process, the opposite of a sudden arrival.

context: The assertion that "an empty house is heavier than a full one" is best understood as:

choices.text: a deliberate paradox in which weight stands for emotional difficulty
a literal observation about how sound carries in a bare room
an exaggeration the narrator immediately admits is untrue
a practical warning about the labor of moving furniture

why.A: Correct — the claim contradicts ordinary sense, and the sentences that follow relocate the weight to "somewhere harder to carry," which makes the burden felt rather than physical.
why.B: Acoustics never come up, and the narrator ties the heaviness to what packing removes, not to what a bare room sounds like.
why.C: She does not retract it; she elaborates on it, saying the three-quarters-boxed kitchen pressed on her more than before.
why.D: The labor of packing is real in the passage, but the narrator's point is that the room grew heavier as it emptied, which no amount of lifting explains.

context: The passage's closing image, in which the narrator hears the third stair "clearing its throat," achieves its effect by:

choices.text: returning to the house's voice from the opening paragraph and treating it as still speaking
revealing that the narrator has moved back into her grandmother's house
suggesting that the narrator has begun to doubt her own memory
introducing a new character who has been listening from the stairs

why.A: Correct — the opening gives the house creaks, drafts, and a groan from the third stair, and the ending gives that same stair a throat to clear, so the house is still addressing her from forty miles away.
why.B: She says the spoons are in a drawer in her own kitchen and the stair is forty miles off, so she has not returned.
why.C: The image is presented as something she hears rather than something she questions, and nothing casts doubt on her recollection.
why.D: No person is introduced; the sound belongs to the stair, which the passage has treated as part of the house's voice from the first paragraph.

context: Nadia's reaction to her brother's age is compared to being startled "the way you are startled by your own voice on a recording" in order to suggest that she finds the fact:

choices.text: familiar and strange at the same time, because it concerns her as much as him
embarrassing to admit to anyone outside the family
impossible to believe without seeing documentation
less important than the other changes she has been through

why.A: Correct — a recorded voice is unmistakably your own and still sounds wrong, and Amir turning forty-four means Nadia is aging too, so the comparison folds her into the surprise.
why.B: The comparison concerns a private jolt of recognition, and nothing in the scene suggests she is worried about outside opinion.
why.C: The narrator says she keeps forgetting and being startled, not that she doubts the fact.
why.D: The passage lists her own changes separately; this comparison is about the shock itself, not about ranking it below anything.

context: In writing that the clove cigarettes their father quit in 1998 left a smell "whose ghost had never left the front room," the narrator conveys that:

choices.text: a trace of him persists in the house long after the habit ended
the family believes the house is genuinely haunted
their father continued smoking in secret for years afterward
the front room has been sealed off and left unused

why.A: Correct — calling the lingering smell a ghost makes it a remnant that outlasts its source, which fits a habit abandoned decades earlier and still faintly detectable.
why.B: The word is figurative; the passage treats the smell as a physical trace, and no character suggests a haunting.
why.C: The passage gives 1998 as the year he quit and offers nothing to undercut it.
why.D: Nadia stands in the entryway and the room is part of the house they are sorting, so it is not sealed off.

context: The narrator writes that "The arithmetic of it had never balanced" to describe the relationship between Nadia and Amir. This figure of speech emphasizes that:

choices.text: the two siblings contributed to their father unequally, and both knew it
the siblings disagreed about how much the house was worth
Nadia had sent less money than she had promised to send
their father had divided his property unfairly between them

why.A: Correct — the sentence follows a list of what Amir did over eleven years against what Nadia did, and the accounting image names the imbalance they both recognized and never discussed.
why.B: Valuation never comes up; the imbalance described is one of time and presence.
why.C: The passage says she sent money and called on birthdays without suggesting she fell short of a promise.
why.D: The figure describes what the siblings gave, not what their father left behind.

context: The maple in the side yard, remembered as "a stick of a thing tied to a stake" and now tall enough to shade the house, most likely functions as:

choices.text: a measure of how much time has passed since the family arrived
evidence that the property has been poorly maintained
a sign that Nadia intends to sell the house quickly
a reminder of an argument the siblings had as children

why.A: Correct — Nadia remembers it being planted the spring after they arrived, so its growth from a staked stick to full shade marks the same span the photograph and her father's 1971 arrival establish.
why.B: A tree that has grown tall enough to shade a wall is a sign of years passing, not of neglect.
why.C: Her plans for the house are left unresolved, and the tree is tied to memory rather than to any decision.
why.D: No argument involving the tree is mentioned; what she recalls is its planting.

context: The narrator describes the bakery's finances as "a slow leak she had mistaken for a business." This comparison is used to:

choices.text: capture the harshness of the judgment the narrator made at nineteen
explain a physical problem with the bakery building
show that Mr. Callan shared the narrator's view of the loan
present the mother's own assessment of what she was doing

why.A: Correct — the phrase comes from the speech the narrator delivered in the car at nineteen while having opinions, and the rest of the passage is spent revising it.
why.B: The leak is figurative, standing for money steadily lost; no damage to the building is mentioned.
why.C: Mr. Callan grants the loan every year and speaks of what the town needs, so he does not treat it as a mistake.
why.D: The mother answers that she is not arguing with the arithmetic but also counting other things, which is a different assessment from the narrator's.

context: Mr. Callan says the town needs "somewhere that smells like something in February." He uses this phrasing to identify the bakery as:

choices.text: a source of ordinary comfort during the emptiest part of the year
the only building in town with working heat in winter
a business that could attract tourists earlier in the season
a place whose ventilation problems the town had long tolerated

why.A: Correct — February falls in the months the passage describes as emptied of everyone but the crews and the eleven families, and naming a smell rather than a product makes the bakery a comfort rather than a transaction.
why.B: He speaks of smell, not warmth, and no comparison between buildings is made.
why.C: His remark is about the off-season itself; the passage treats summer tourists as a separate matter the loan cannot fix.
why.D: The smell he names is the appeal of the place, not a defect.

context: The narrator writes that on the drive home his mother "let me sit with it for about ten miles." Measuring the pause this way primarily conveys:

choices.text: that she allowed a long silence to pass before responding
that the two of them were lost and driving without direction
that she was concentrating too hard on the road to speak
that the argument continued for most of the drive

why.A: Correct — the drive is forty minutes each way, so ten miles of it is a substantial stretch, and giving the silence a distance rather than a duration stresses how long she let it run.
why.B: The route is a familiar annual one between Wexford and home, and no confusion about direction is suggested.
why.C: The passage attributes the silence to her deliberate choice, introduced by her letting him sit with it.
why.D: The narrator had already finished speaking before this pause; what fills the ten miles is silence, not argument.

context: According to the passage, when investigators grew the fungus by itself, it produced:

choices.text: a formless mat.
a thin green smear.
a layered, weatherproof body.
an outer rind and a loose interior.

why.A: The third paragraph is explicit: "Alone, the fungus produced a formless mat and the alga a thin green smear."
why.B: That is what the alga produced alone. The sentence names both results, and this is the other one.
why.C: The layered body appeared only when the two were brought back together under the right moisture and light.
why.D: The rind and the loose interior are parts of the finished lichen described in the fourth paragraph, not of the fungus grown alone.

context: The passage presents which finding as having settled the dispute over whether a lichen is a single organism?

choices.text: Separating the two partners, growing each alone, and recombining them into the familiar layered body.
The discovery under the microscope that lichen tissue contains two kinds of cell.
The demonstration that lichen acids dissolve the mineral surfaces the organism sits on.
The later discovery of a yeast embedded in the outer layer of many lichens.

why.A: The third paragraph says settling the question "required patience rather than argument", and the patience described is the separate-and-recombine work. Producing the whole organism from two cultured parts is what the critics’ objections could not survive.
why.B: The microscope raised the proposal. The passage then spends a paragraph on why that evidence alone was resisted, so it cannot be what settled the matter.
why.C: The acids explain how the partnership works, and appear after the dispute has already been described as settled.
why.D: The yeast is later work, and the passage offers it as unsettling the picture further rather than as resolving the original argument.

context: The passage suggests that lichens can serve as a record of air quality mainly because they:

choices.text: take in material directly from the air and cannot get rid of it.
grow faster in places where the air is clean.
change colour in proportion to the sulfur around them.
are found only in regions that have never been industrialised.

why.A: Two facts in the sixth paragraph combine: having no roots, lichens absorb across their whole surface, and "they cannot shed what they absorb". Retention is what turns an organism into a record.
why.B: The passage never links growth rate to air quality. It links which species survive to air quality.
why.C: The change described is in the composition of the community — which species remain — not in the colour of an individual.
why.D: The passage describes surveys in places where sulfur compounds are heavy, so lichens plainly occur in industrial regions.

context: According to the seventh paragraph, the two reproductive strategies differ mainly in whether:

choices.text: the dispersing unit already contains both partners.
the lichen reproduces in wind or through animals.
the fungus or the alga initiates the process.
reproduction happens in wet conditions or dry ones.

why.A: A spore "carries none of its partner with it" and must find an alga; the bundles arrive "complete". Whether both partners travel together is the whole of the difference.
why.B: Wind and passing animals are both named as ways the same bundles travel, so they do not separate the two strategies.
why.C: The paragraph describes the fungus as the one reproducing in both cases.
why.D: Moisture appears in the third paragraph as a condition for assembly, not as a difference between the two strategies.

context: The phrase "a slow machine for making soil" serves mainly to:

choices.text: cast a scattered set of small effects as one piece of steady, purposeful work.
suggest that lichens were engineered for a particular function.
emphasise how little soil a single lichen can produce.
contrast biological processes with industrial ones.

why.A: The sentences after it list etching, trapping dust, and accumulating debris over centuries. Calling that a machine gathers separate slow effects into one process with an output.
why.B: The passage treats the arrangement as something that evolved, and nothing in the paragraph implies design.
why.C: The paragraph stresses that the process works — "the reason that bare rock does not stay bare" — not that its yield is negligible.
why.D: No industrial process is mentioned. "Machine" is doing metaphorical work, not setting up a comparison.

context: The passage as a whole is organised to:

choices.text: establish a correction to an old classification, then trace what followed from it.
alternate between the arguments of the critics and those of their opponents.
move backwards from a present-day use of lichens to the discovery behind it.
compare lichens with other organisms that live in partnerships.

why.A: The first three paragraphs establish the misfiling and the evidence that overturned it. Everything after — division of labour, soil, air quality, reproduction, the boundary of individuality — follows from the organism being a partnership.
why.B: The critics appear in one paragraph and are answered in the same one. There is no alternation.
why.C: The order runs forward: the nineteenth century first, the later work last.
why.D: No other partnership organism is discussed. The yeast in the final paragraph is a third partner inside lichens, not a comparison case.

context: The author’s attitude toward the botanists who first classified lichens as plants is best described as:

choices.text: willing to explain how a reasonable error arose without defending the conclusion.
openly scornful of their inattention.
indifferent to whether their reasoning was sound.
admiring of a classification that later work confirmed.

why.A: The first paragraph grants that lichens "looked like modest vegetation" and calls the result "tidy" — then, in the same breath, "completely mistaken". The third paragraph extends the same courtesy to the critics, whose resistance "was not unreasonable".
why.B: Scorn would not bother to explain why the mistake was easy to make, and "filed them among the plants and moved on" is the sharpest phrasing in the passage.
why.C: The passage sets out the critics’ two arguments in detail, which is the opposite of indifference to their reasoning.
why.D: The classification was overturned, and the passage says so in its second sentence.

context: The passage is best described as an account of:

choices.text: a young man discovering that his mother’s job consisted largely of obligations no record held.
a family business failing after the closure of the mills.
a summer spent learning to drive a delivery van efficiently.
a disagreement between a mother and son over how a route should be run.

why.A: The narrator memorises the streets in a week and then spends the rest of the summer learning the rest: the extra loaves, the porch in winter, the tomatoes. "None of it was in the ledger" states the passage’s subject outright.
why.B: The mills appear in one sentence as background. The route is still running, and nothing in the passage suggests it is failing.
why.C: He has the driving in hand by the end of the first week, which the passage treats as the least of what the job requires.
why.D: Mother and son never disagree. The closest thing to a correction is her remark about Ridge Road, and she is pleased.

context: According to the passage, the narrator’s mother had driven the route for:

choices.text: nineteen years.
twenty years.
nine years.
forty-one years.

why.A: The first sentence gives nineteen years, and the last paragraph repeats it.
why.B: Twenty is the narrator’s age, given in the third paragraph.
why.C: Nine miles is the distance to the next grocery, not a span of years.
why.D: Forty-one is the number of stops on the route.

context: The grocery owner’s behaviour at the fourth stop most strongly suggests that he:

choices.text: was more interested in the narrator’s mother than in getting the facts right.
resented having to deal with an inexperienced driver.
had been misinformed about the nature of her injury.
wanted to delay the delivery until he had cleared shelf space.

why.A: He asks three questions about "a surgery my mother had not had" and nods at bad answers "as though I had been some help". The questions are a way of attending to her, and their accuracy is beside the point.
why.B: He comes out to the curb before the van is open and stays talking, which is welcome rather than resentful.
why.C: The passage gives no source of misinformation, and his satisfaction with wrong answers shows the facts were not what he was after.
why.D: He takes the tray immediately and holds it throughout, so nothing is being delayed.

context: The one-sentence paragraph "The ledger recorded loaves." functions mainly to:

choices.text: set the formal record against the arrangements the preceding paragraph has just described.
indicate that the narrator had begun keeping the books himself.
suggest that the mother had been careless about her paperwork.
introduce the financial difficulty the route was in.

why.A: It lands immediately after Mr. Alves’s extra loaves and the storm porch on Ridge Road, and immediately after "None of it was in the ledger." Its brevity is the point: the record holds one thing, the job holds many.
why.B: The narrator never describes doing the books; he describes driving and delivering.
why.C: Nothing suggests the ledger was kept badly. It recorded exactly what a ledger records.
why.D: No financial difficulty appears anywhere in the passage.

context: As it is used in the phrase "a circuit of small accounts, most of them not in money," the word accounts most nearly means:

choices.text: ongoing obligations.
financial records.
spoken descriptions.
customer complaints.

why.A: The clause "most of them not in money" rules out the financial sense on purpose, and the examples that follow — extra loaves for news, bread left in a porch — are debts of a non-monetary kind.
why.B: That is the sense the sentence explicitly sets aside, and the ledger sentence two paragraphs later marks the difference.
why.C: An account in the sense of a narrative would not be described as being "in money" or not.
why.D: No one in the passage complains. The arrangements are willing on both sides.

context: The narrator’s understanding in August differs from his understanding in June chiefly in that by August he recognises the arrangements as:

choices.text: choices his mother made repeatedly rather than simply how things were done.
inefficiencies that a new driver could reasonably remove.
obligations imposed on his mother by her customers.
a system his mother had designed before he was born.

why.A: The final paragraph turns on exactly this: "I had not thought of it as a decision. That, I understand now, is what she was telling me: that it had been one, every time, for nineteen years."
why.B: He continues every arrangement he inherits, including the one that is no longer necessary in summer.
why.C: Mrs. Ferreira presses tomatoes on him and Mr. Alves offers news; the exchanges run both ways rather than being imposed.
why.D: The passage presents the arrangements as having accumulated one at a time, not as a design.

context: The passage is organised as:

choices.text: a narrator recounting a past summer while commenting on it from a later vantage point.
a strictly chronological account with no later commentary.
a series of character sketches framed by a single conversation.
an argument supported by episodes drawn from several summers.

why.A: The events run from June to August, but phrases like "It took me most of June to understand" and "That, I understand now" are spoken by someone who already knows how the summer ends.
why.B: The chronology is there, but so is the later voice, which the final paragraph makes explicit.
why.C: Mr. Alves and Mrs. Ferreira are sketched briefly, and no single conversation frames the passage.
why.D: One summer is described, and the passage tells rather than argues.

context: The narrator’s attitude toward his twenty-year-old self is best described as:

choices.text: amused at his confidence without being harsh about it.
embarrassed to the point of dismissing everything he did.
defensive about how quickly he learned the route.
indifferent, reporting his actions without evaluation.

why.A: "The unearned confidence of someone who has recently learned to parallel park" is affectionate mockery, and the closing clause — later than she hoped, earlier than she feared — grades him gently in both directions.
why.B: He credits himself with noticing, and with keeping the porch arrangement up past winter.
why.C: He offers the week it took him to memorise the streets as evidence of how little that mattered, not as a defence.
why.D: Nearly every sentence about his younger self carries an evaluation; the closing paragraph is almost entirely evaluation.

context: Which detail best supports the idea that the narrator’s mother intended him to work the route out for himself?

choices.text: She rode along in August "with her hands in her lap and said almost nothing, which was its own kind of instruction."
She warned him that Mrs. Ferreira would try to give him tomatoes.
She handed him the keys when her wrist gave out.
She asked whether he had kept up the Ridge Road arrangement.

why.A: The narrator names the silence as instruction. Choosing not to explain, while present and able to, is the clearest evidence of intent in the passage.
why.B: The tomato warning is one of the few things she does explain, so it works against the claim rather than for it.
why.C: Handing over the keys was forced by the injury; the passage gives it no pedagogical purpose.
why.D: That question comes after the summer is over and confirms what he did. It is the test of the lesson, not evidence of the intention behind it.

context: The comparison of the keys to "a pair of glasses you have worn so long you have stopped seeing through them" conveys mainly that the mother:

choices.text: no longer noticed the route as something separate from herself.
had grown careless about the quality of her work.
was reluctant to give up control of the business.
could no longer see well enough to drive safely.

why.A: Glasses worn that long are looked *with*, not *at*. The image says the route had stopped being a thing she could describe — which is why the instructions she gives are so thin.
why.B: Everything that follows shows the work being done with care, most of it unrecorded.
why.C: She hands the keys over in the first sentence without any resistance.
why.D: Her wrist is what gave out; the image is about familiarity, not eyesight.

context: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: why a very small charge produced a large change, and what that does and does not prove.
establishing that disposable bags are more harmful than reusable ones.
arguing that governments should replace bag charges with bonuses.
tracing the history of environmental regulation in cities.

why.A: It opens with the gap between the prediction and the result, weighs two explanations, brings in the bonus experiment to separate them, and closes on what the case does and does not generalise to.
why.B: Environmental harm is never discussed. The passage is about behaviour and incentives.
why.C: Bonuses appear as a comparison that worked worse, which is the opposite of a recommendation.
why.D: No history is given; no dates or jurisdictions are named.

context: According to the passage, where bag charges have been introduced, bag use commonly falls by:

choices.text: seventy per cent or more within a month.
about ten per cent within a year.
five per cent, matching the size of the bonus.
an amount too small to measure.

why.A: Stated in the first paragraph, along with the fact that the reduction holds rather than rebounding.
why.B: Ten is the number of cents charged, not a percentage, and the passage gives no one-year figure.
why.C: Five cents is the size of the bonus in the comparison study, not a reduction in bag use.
why.D: That describes the bonus result in two studies, not the charge result.

context: The two explanations offered in the passage differ mainly over whether:

choices.text: the size of the charge matters at all.
bag use actually fell after the charge was introduced.
shoppers are aware that a charge exists.
cities are entitled to impose such charges.

why.A: The first says a one-cent charge "would do nearly as much work"; the second says the amount "matters somewhat", because it has to read as deliberate. That is the axis they disagree on.
why.B: Both accounts are attempts to explain the fall, so both take it as given.
why.C: Both require the shopper to notice the charge — as a moment of choice, or as a signal.
why.D: Entitlement is a question of policy authority, which the passage never raises.

context: The paragraph describing jurisdictions that offered a five-cent bonus functions mainly to:

choices.text: supply a case that pulls the two explanations apart.
show that both explanations were mistaken.
introduce a policy the author prefers to the charge.
illustrate how difficult it is to measure shopping behaviour.

why.A: The paragraph before it says the two accounts "are difficult to separate, because most policies deliver both effects at once", and this one is introduced as the case that "came closer than most".
why.B: The result damages the first explanation "on its own" and fits the second, so it discriminates between them rather than refuting both.
why.C: The bonus performed worse, and the author treats that as informative rather than desirable.
why.D: The measurements are reported without complaint; what is difficult is separating causes, not measuring effects.

context: The bonus result is presented as a difficulty for the first explanation because:

choices.text: a bonus creates a moment of choice as surely as a charge does, yet produced far less change.
the bonus was smaller than the charge.
shoppers in those jurisdictions already owned reusable bags.
the bonus was offered only to shoppers who asked for it.

why.A: The passage says so directly: "the shopper is asked at the register either way." If attention alone were doing the work, the two should have performed alike, and they did not.
why.B: Five cents against ten is a difference the first explanation dismisses, since on that account the amount is "close to irrelevant".
why.C: The passage never says this, and it would explain a smaller effect for both instruments, not just one.
why.D: Nothing indicates the bonus had to be requested; it is described as given to shoppers who brought their own bags.

context: As it is used in the phrase "hard for the first explanation to accommodate," the word accommodate most nearly means:

choices.text: account for.
provide lodging for.
adapt itself to please.
make room by moving aside.

why.A: The sentence is about whether an explanation can absorb an awkward result and still stand. Explaining the result is what it would have to do.
why.B: The literal lodging sense has no application to an explanation.
why.C: An explanation obliging someone would be a different claim, and the paragraph is about evidence rather than about anyone’s preferences.
why.D: Making room physically is closer to the lodging sense and, again, not something an explanation does.

context: The passage is organised by:

choices.text: presenting a puzzle, weighing two explanations, introducing a case that separates them, and then marking the limits of the finding.
listing the effects of several environmental policies in order of size.
defending a single explanation against objections raised in turn.
comparing one city’s experience with another’s in detail.

why.A: That is the sequence exactly: the gap between prediction and result, the two accounts, the bonus experiment, and the closing paragraphs on cups and on what the case establishes.
why.B: Only bags and cups appear, and they are not ranked.
why.C: The author does not defend one account from the outset; the second is preferred only after the evidence arrives.
why.D: No city is named or described in detail.

context: The author’s attitude toward small charges as a policy instrument is best described as:

choices.text: persuaded that they worked here, and careful about generalising from it.
enthusiastic about applying them wherever possible.
sceptical that the reported reductions occurred at all.
neutral, declining to draw any conclusion.

why.A: The final two paragraphs do both jobs: "not that small charges are a general instrument", and then a narrower claim the author calls "still useful".
why.B: The cup paragraph is an explicit warning against that, noting annoyance and avoidance as the failure modes.
why.C: The reductions are reported as established fact and used as the starting point.
why.D: The passage ends with a stated conclusion about the most common error in designing such policies.

context: Which finding does the passage offer as evidence that small charges are not a general instrument?

choices.text: Charges on disposable cups have worked in some cities and failed in others.
Bag use fell by seventy per cent or more wherever charges were introduced.
A five-cent bonus produced no measurable reduction in two studies.
Losses are felt more sharply than equivalent gains.

why.A: It is introduced as the reason "attempts to reproduce the bag result elsewhere have been uneven", and the passage supplies the mechanism: whether a usable alternative is already in the shopper’s possession.
why.B: That is the consistent result the passage is trying to explain, so it cannot be evidence of unevenness.
why.C: The bonus result separates the two explanations of why the charge worked. It says nothing about where charges transfer.
why.D: That is a psychological principle the passage draws on, not a finding about the reach of the policy.

context: The passage’s closing sentences suggest that a policymaker designing an incentive is most likely to go wrong by:

choices.text: assuming that a bigger number will produce a bigger effect.
setting the charge lower than the public will tolerate.
relying on evidence from a single city.
choosing a charge when a bonus would be cheaper.

why.A: The last two sentences name the error: not "setting the number too low", but "treating the number as the thing that matters" — which is the assumption that size and effect track each other.
why.B: The passage explicitly rejects this as the common error in the sentence before its conclusion.
why.C: Evidence from several jurisdictions is cited, and the unevenness of the cup results is presented as instructive rather than as a methodological warning.
why.D: Cost to the treasury is never discussed, and the bonus is reported as the weaker instrument.

context: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: a verification requirement that was poorly designed, and the unrelated change that eventually made it unnecessary.
the working conditions of children employed in Massachusetts textile mills.
the career of an inspector whose accuracy was recognized in her own lifetime.
the history of birth registration across the United States.

why.A: The passage sets up the affidavit as the wrong instrument for the job, gives Farrow’s diagnosis of why, and then shows the problem dissolving when registries arrived for entirely different reasons.
why.B: The mills are the setting. The passage never describes what the work was like, only how the children’s ages were established.
why.C: The accuracy is established in the final paragraph, and the passage is explicit that it is read for now, not something she was recognized for then.
why.D: Registration appears only in the single paragraph explaining why it spread, and only as it bears on the age question.

context: According to the passage, the law Farrow enforced permitted an employer to establish a child’s age by producing:

choices.text: an affidavit from a parent.
a birth certificate issued by the state.
the inspector’s written judgment.
a physician’s examination.

why.A: The first paragraph says the law "permitted an employer to satisfy an inspector with an affidavit from a parent".
why.B: The passage says most of these families had no certificate, which is the whole reason the affidavit existed.
why.C: Farrow recorded her judgment in a second column of her own, not as something the law recognized.
why.D: No physician appears anywhere in the passage.

context: The passage suggests that a mother who swore to an inaccurate age most often did so because she:

choices.text: did not know the date and gave a figure she had reason to think was close enough.
had been instructed what to say by the mill’s management.
was concealing a birth certificate she actually possessed.
expected no one would ever check the claim against a record.

why.A: The second paragraph says a mother asked to swear "often did not know it", and would give an age she "had every reason to believe was close enough".
why.B: No pressure from employers is described. Farrow’s account locates the problem in the record, not in coercion.
why.C: The passage says many families had no certificate at all, so there was usually nothing to conceal.
why.D: There was no record to check against, which is the point — not that checking was being evaded.

context: Farrow’s 1913 memorandum implies that she regarded false swearing as:

choices.text: a symptom of a recording failure rather than the underlying problem.
the most serious offense an inspector was likely to encounter.
impossible to detect without a physician’s help.
less common than other inspectors believed it to be.

why.A: Her proposed remedy was a registry rather than a stiffer penalty for false swearing, which only makes sense if she thought the swearing was downstream of the missing record.
why.B: Treating it as the gravest offense would have pointed her toward penalties, which is the remedy she specifically did not propose.
why.C: She judged ages herself, without a physician, and did so accurately.
why.D: She reports disagreement in more than two visits in three, which is a high rate, not a low one.

context: The fourth paragraph functions primarily to:

choices.text: show that the remedy Farrow wanted arrived for reasons that had nothing to do with her argument.
describe the actuarial methods the insurance industry was developing.
establish the date on which Farrow left the inspectorate.
contrast conditions in the northeast with conditions elsewhere.

why.A: It lists pensions, the draft and insurance as the motives, and then says outright that the question stopped "not because anyone won the argument".
why.B: The actuarial tables are named in a single clause as one motive among three, and are never described.
why.C: Her departure in 1919 belongs to the following paragraph.
why.D: The northeast is mentioned once to bound a claim about coverage, not to set up a regional comparison.

context: The passage is organized as:

choices.text: a problem, one official’s diagnosis of it, and the unrelated development that dissolved it.
a chronological biography of a single public official.
a comparison of two competing pieces of legislation.
a summary of evidence followed by a rebuttal of it.

why.A: The gap between the two columns is the problem, the 1913 memorandum is the diagnosis, and the registry paragraph is the development that ends the problem without resolving the argument.
why.B: A biography would not end with the subject "difficult to follow" and the ledgers read for a purpose she did not intend.
why.C: Only one law is described, and the registry is not presented as competing legislation.
why.D: Nothing in the passage is rebutted. The final paragraph adds a finding rather than answering one.

context: The author’s attitude toward Farrow is best described as:

choices.text: respectful of her reasoning and candid about how little effect it had.
admiring of her achievements and confident that they were recognized.
skeptical of the accuracy she is now credited with.
detached, treating her as one example among many.

why.A: Her notes are called careful and her judgments accurate, and the passage still says the memorandum "was not acted on" and that no one won the argument.
why.B: The passage says the opposite about recognition — she is difficult to follow after 1919, and the ledgers are read for something she was not trying to show.
why.C: The eighty-percent figure is reported without hedging, and the author raises no doubt about it.
why.D: She is the only person the passage follows, and her reasoning is set out at length.

context: Which detail most directly supports the claim that Farrow’s judgments of age were reliable?

choices.text: Her judged ages matched certificates issued later within a year about eighty percent of the time.
She kept forty-one ledgers over the course of her career.
Her memorandum circulated among inspectors in 1913.
She told a state commission that she looked at the hands.

why.A: This is a check of her judgments against an independent record made afterward, which is what evidence of accuracy has to be.
why.B: The number of ledgers shows how much she recorded, not whether what she recorded was right.
why.C: Circulation shows her argument was read, which is a separate matter from her accuracy.
why.D: That remark describes her method, or rather her inability to describe it, and establishes nothing about the results.

context: As used in the final paragraph, "follow" most nearly means:

choices.text: trace the later course of.
obey.
understand.
come after in sequence.

why.A: The sentence concerns what became of Farrow after 1919, so following her means tracking where she went.
why.B: Obeying would require an instruction, and nothing in the sentence issues one.
why.C: The difficulty is in locating her afterward, not in making sense of her.
why.D: That sense needs two things in an order, and the sentence names only Farrow.

context: The passage draws its central distinction between:

choices.text: certifying a fact and having recorded that fact in the first place.
state law and municipal ordinance.
an inspector’s authority and an employer’s.
the northeast and the rest of the country.

why.A: Farrow’s argument is that the affidavit "asked a parent to certify a fact the state had never bothered to record" — the certifying and the recording are precisely what the passage separates.
why.B: The passage mentions the city and the states but never sets their laws against each other.
why.C: The affidavit is what the employer produces and the inspector accepts, so the two are not in conflict over authority.
why.D: The one regional reference bounds a claim about coverage and is not developed into a contrast.

context: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: a decision about what to uncover in a layered panel, and the competing principles behind it.
the technical methods conservators use to image paintings without damaging them.
the attribution of a Nativity to a follower of Gerard David.
the practice of overpainting in sixteenth-century workshops.

why.A: The discovery opens the passage, two opposed positions occupy its middle, and the department’s decision and its justification close it.
why.B: Infrared and X-ray appear once, as the form the published record took, and are never explained.
why.C: The attribution is given in the first paragraph as background and is never questioned or argued about.
why.D: Overpainting appears only inside the second position’s argument, as a reason the top layer is itself a restoration.

context: According to the passage, the layer found directly on the bare oak was:

choices.text: a drawing.
a ground with no image on it.
an earlier Nativity.
the 1520 Nativity.

why.A: The first paragraph works downward and ends "on the bare oak, a drawing".
why.B: The blank ground is the layer immediately above the drawing, not the one on the wood.
why.C: The earlier Nativity is the second layer from the top.
why.D: The 1520 Nativity is the visible surface, the layer furthest from the oak.

context: The second position would most likely object to the first position on the grounds that it:

choices.text: grants authority to the topmost layer without any reason beyond its being topmost.
underestimates how difficult removing a layer of paint actually is.
assumes the lower paintings are of higher artistic quality.
disregards the costume evidence used to date the panel.

why.A: The fourth paragraph puts this as a question: why should the last hand to touch a panel have more authority than the first? That is an objection to the rule, not to the painting.
why.B: Technical difficulty is never raised by either position.
why.C: The passage says explicitly that the second position "does not hold that older is better".
why.D: The costume dating is stated once as background and neither position disputes it.

context: The statement that the drawing on the oak "was never meant to be seen" serves to:

choices.text: support the first position’s view that not everything beneath a surface belongs to the finished work.
explain why infrared imaging was needed to find it.
establish that the drawing came from a different hand than the paintings.
cast doubt on the attribution to a follower of Gerard David.

why.A: It closes the paragraph setting out the first position, and it does the work of distinguishing the finished object from the working notes underneath it.
why.B: The imaging is described two paragraphs later and for a different reason.
why.C: The passage never says who made the drawing.
why.D: The attribution concerns the top layer, which this sentence is not about.

context: The passage is organized as:

choices.text: a discovery, two opposed positions on what to do about it, and the resolution actually adopted.
a chronological account of a single restoration project from start to finish.
a general principle illustrated by a series of comparable cases.
an argument for one position and a rebuttal of the other.

why.A: Paragraph one is the discovery, paragraphs three and four are the two positions, and the last two give the decision and the conservator’s account of it.
why.B: The passage skips most of the project and spends its length on an argument rather than a sequence of events.
why.C: Only one case is discussed. The author says the argument recurs but gives no other instance.
why.D: The author argues for neither position and says the decision satisfied neither.

context: The author’s treatment of the second position is best described as:

choices.text: deliberately even-handed, noting that it is usually presented less carefully than it deserves.
dismissive, treating it as a caricature of a serious view.
enthusiastic, endorsing it over the first position.
so neutral that the position is never actually stated.

why.A: The paragraph opens by saying the position "is less easily caricatured than it is usually made to sound", and then states it carefully — the remark is a correction of how it is usually handled.
why.B: The author names the caricature in order to set it aside, which is the opposite of endorsing it.
why.C: The passage gives the first position an equally careful hearing and endorses neither.
why.D: The position is stated at length, including the question it rests on.

context: Which statement best supports the senior conservator’s claim that the decision was not a compromise?

choices.text: The department concluded that the panel’s value as an object and its value as evidence were different things, only one of which required removing paint.
The decision satisfied neither of the two positions.
The argument occupied the department for two years before a decision was reached.
The imaging was published at full resolution rather than as illustrations.

why.A: Her definition is that a compromise splits a difference. Separating two values and answering each on its own terms is not splitting anything, which is exactly why she refuses the word.
why.B: Satisfying neither side is what a compromise usually looks like, so this points the other way.
why.C: How long the argument took says nothing about the shape of its conclusion.
why.D: The resolution of the images shows how thorough the record is, not why the decision was principled.

context: As used in the fourth paragraph, "authoritative" most nearly means:

choices.text: entitled to be treated as the definitive version.
issued by an official body.
commanding in manner or appearance.
strictly and consistently enforced.

why.A: The sentence asks why the topmost layer should count as the painting, so the word is about which version has the final claim.
why.B: No official body issued any layer of the panel.
why.C: That sense describes a person’s bearing, and the subject here is a layer of paint.
why.D: Enforcement belongs to rules, and the passage is asking which object is the work.

context: It can reasonably be inferred that the published images allow the lower paintings to be:

choices.text: studied in detail even though they will remain covered.
shown to visitors alongside the 1520 Nativity.
dated more precisely than the visible surface.
removed and remounted on separate panels.

why.A: The passage says the lower paintings "can be studied by anyone, and will never be seen", which is only possible because the record exists apart from the object.
why.B: They remain under the paint. What hangs is still the 1520 Nativity.
why.C: No dates are given for the lower layers at all.
why.D: Removing them is precisely what the department decided against.

context: The two positions described in the passage differ most fundamentally over:

choices.text: what gives one layer of a panel a better claim than another to be the work itself.
whether the lower layers are worth documenting at all.
how much weight costume evidence should carry in dating a panel.
whether removing an upper layer is technically achievable.

why.A: The first position takes the last coherent state; the second asks why last should mean authoritative. Both are answers to the same question about which layer counts.
why.B: The first position calls the lower layers "worth recording, worth publishing", so documentation is common ground.
why.C: Neither position raises the costume dating, which appears only as background.
why.D: Both assume removal is possible — the first objects that it would destroy the visible painting, which presupposes it could be done.
